section: High Courts and subordinate judiciary; judicial review, judicial activism, PIL and judicial overreach debate
subsections: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs

accepted.s: Which one of the following best describes the relaxation associated with locus standi in Public Interest Litigation?
o: Any public-spirited citizen may approach the court on behalf of persons unable to do so
A petition can be filed only after approval by Parliament
Only a government officer may file a petition
Only the directly injured person may approach the court
accepted.x: PIL relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi, enabling a public-spirited citizen to move the court for persons who cannot approach it themselves.
accepted.tq: Apply the meaning of ‘place to stand’ to identify who may approach the court.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the development of Public Interest Litigation in India:
1. It grew out of judicial activism.
2. It was an outcome of judicial restraint.
3. It democratised access to courts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: PIL developed through judicial activism and helped democratise access to courts. It was not an outcome of judicial restraint.
accepted.tq: Reject the reversed conceptual pair and retain the two positively stated consequences.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Who filed the first Public Interest Litigation case, Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, in 1979?
accepted.x: Kapila Hingorani filed Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, the first major PIL case, concerning the rights of undertrial prisoners.
accepted.tq: Match the landmark case with the person who initiated it.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The expression ‘Mother of PILs’ is associated with
accepted.x: Kapila Hingorani is known as the ‘Mother of PILs’ because she filed the Hussainara Khatoon case on behalf of undertrial prisoners.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the petitioner, judges and litigant in the same landmark case.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, decided in 1979, primarily concerned the
o: right to speedy trial of undertrial prisoners
accepted.x: The Hussainara Khatoon case focused on the right of undertrial prisoners to a speedy trial.
accepted.tq: Link the landmark case to its distinctive constitutional issue.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Hussainara Khatoon case — disclosure of candidates’ assets and education
accepted.x: The disclosure of candidates’ assets and education was dealt with in the affidavit case. Hussainara Khatoon concerned speedy trial for undertrial prisoners.
accepted.tq: Find the swapped subject associated with a landmark case.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Hussainara Khatoon case
B. S.P. Gupta case
C. Vishaka case
D. M.C. Mehta environmental cases
accepted.x: Hussainara Khatoon was decided in 1979, S.P. Gupta in 1981, M.C. Mehta environmental cases followed, and Vishaka was decided in 1997.
accepted.tq: Fix the dated endpoints first and place the intervening PIL developments between them.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The expression ‘epistolary jurisdiction’ in the context of PIL refers to the practice of treating which of the following as petitions?
o: Only affidavits filed by government departments
Police charge sheets and audit reports
accepted.x: Under epistolary jurisdiction, courts treated letters and postcards as writ petitions and also acted on newspaper reports indicating violations of rights.
accepted.tq: Identify the exact forms of informal communication accepted by courts.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
With reference to Public Interest Litigation, consider the following statements:
1. It may be filed under Article 32 before the Supreme Court.
2. It may be filed under Article 226 before a High Court.
3. It can be initiated only by the person whose fundamental right has been directly violated.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: PIL may be filed under Articles 32 and 226. The third statement is false because locus standi is relaxed and a public-spirited citizen may approach the court for others.
accepted.tq: Separate the constitutional remedies from the deliberately narrow description of standing.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following judges, apart from Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati, helped lay the foundation for judicial activism?
o: O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai
accepted.x: Justices O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai are identified as having laid the base of judicial activism along with the better-known PIL pioneers.
accepted.tq: Distinguish judicial contributors from cases and litigants.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following is a major negative consequence associated with the increasing misuse of Public Interest Litigation?
o: Removal of locus standi from constitutional law
Transfer of all cases to Lok Adalats
accepted.x: Although PIL democratised access to courts, its misuse has also contributed to the overburdening of courts.
accepted.tq: Balance the stated positive and negative consequences instead of choosing an extreme institutional effect.
accepted.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which Article declares that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void?
accepted.x: Article 13 provides that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void, including pre-Constitution laws to the extent of inconsistency.
accepted.tq: Associate the constitutional provision with the precise consequence it creates.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The power of the Supreme Court to review its own judgments is provided under
accepted.x: Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review judgments or orders made by it, subject to constitutional and statutory provisions.
accepted.tq: Discriminate among nearby Articles by matching the specific judicial function.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Article 226 differs from Article 32 principally because the High Courts may issue writs under Article 226 for
o: Fundamental Rights and any other purpose
accepted.x: The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 extends to enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, making it wider in scope than Article 32.
accepted.tq: Compare the scope of two similar writ jurisdictions by identifying the additional phrase.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Article 32 enables the Supreme Court to protect Fundamental Rights primarily through
accepted.x: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
accepted.tq: Identify the constitutional remedy linked to the enforcement function.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional basis of judicial review:
1. The expression ‘judicial review’ is expressly defined in the Constitution.
2. The power flows from several constitutional provisions.
3. It is regarded as part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The term ‘judicial review’ is not used in the Constitution, but the power flows from several Articles and is part of the basic structure.
accepted.tq: Distinguish an express constitutional label from a power inferred from several provisions.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Judicial review in India is based on which combination of constitutional features?
o: Collective responsibility, adult suffrage and emergency powers
A written Constitution, federalism and Fundamental Rights
An unwritten constitution, unitary government and parliamentary privilege
accepted.x: Judicial review follows from India’s written Constitution, federal structure and protection of Fundamental Rights.
accepted.tq: Select the combination of structural features that supports the power under examination.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The concept of judicial review in India was borrowed primarily from the Constitution of
accepted.x: The United States is the principal constitutional source of the concept of judicial review adopted in India.
accepted.tq: Separate the source of judicial review from other borrowed parliamentary and federal features.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which statement best explains the difference between the Indian and American approaches to judicial review mentioned in the constitutional comparison?
o: India uses procedure established by law, whereas the United States uses due process
India uses due process, whereas the United States uses procedure established by law
Both systems use identical constitutional language and scope
Neither system permits review of legislative action
accepted.x: India follows ‘procedure established by law’ under Article 21, while the United States employs the broader expression ‘due process’; consequently, Indian review is narrower in this respect.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between two look-alike constitutional phrases.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Indian system of judicial review is described as blending
o: American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty
French administrative supremacy with British federalism
Canadian judicial restraint with Australian parliamentary sovereignty
British judicial supremacy with American parliamentary sovereignty
accepted.x: India combines the American idea of judicial supremacy with the British tradition of parliamentary sovereignty.
accepted.tq: Match each constitutional characteristic with its correct comparative source.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: What was the effect of the 42nd and 43rd Constitutional Amendments on the judicial review power of High Courts?
o: The 42nd Amendment restored the power and the 43rd abolished it
The 42nd Amendment barred review of Central laws by High Courts and the 43rd restored that power
Both Amendments abolished judicial review by High Courts
The 42nd Amendment transferred the power to State Legislatures and the 43rd returned it to Parliament
accepted.x: The 42nd Amendment, 1976, restricted High Courts from reviewing Central laws; the 43rd Amendment, 1977, restored that power.
accepted.tq: Track the reversal by pairing each Amendment with its distinct effect.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following Articles confers original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court in disputes between the Union and the States?
accepted.x: Article 131 provides the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction in specified disputes involving the Union and States.
accepted.tq: Identify the jurisdiction by its constitutional Article rather than by the court exercising it.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Special Leave to Appeal jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is associated with
accepted.x: Article 136 confers the Supreme Court’s special leave jurisdiction, while Articles 132 to 135 deal with specified appellate matters.
accepted.tq: Use the distinctive phrase ‘Special Leave’ to locate the correct Article.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: A Presidential reference seeking the advisory opinion of the Supreme Court is dealt with under
accepted.x: Article 143 provides for the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court on matters referred by the President.
accepted.tq: Match the advisory function with the constitutional authority that initiates it.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The power of superintendence of a High Court over subordinate courts is provided under
accepted.x: Article 227 confers on High Courts the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within their territorial jurisdiction, subject to constitutional limitations.
accepted.tq: Distinguish High Court writ jurisdiction from its supervisory jurisdiction.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 245 makes legislative power subject to the Constitution.
2. Article 246(3) gives the States exclusive power over matters in the State List, subject to the Constitution.
3. Articles 251 and 254 deal with repugnancy between certain laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. Articles 245 and 246 govern legislative competence, while Articles 251 and 254 address inconsistency or repugnancy between laws.
accepted.tq: Test several related Articles as a constitutional-competence cluster.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Under Article 254, a State law that is repugnant to a law made by Parliament is generally
o: void to the extent of the inconsistency
accepted.x: Article 254 embodies the rule of repugnancy: the State law is void to the extent that it is inconsistent with the applicable Parliamentary law.
accepted.tq: Apply the consequence of repugnancy rather than confusing it with legislative privilege.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Article 372(1) is relevant to judicial review because it concerns
o: the appointment of High Court judges
the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
accepted.x: Article 372(1) provides the constitutional basis for continuing pre-Constitution laws subject to their consistency with the Constitution and judicial review.
accepted.tq: Identify the historical category of laws linked to the Article.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised ground of judicial review in India?
o: Contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure
Disagreement with the policy preference of the majority party
accepted.x: The recognised grounds include violation of Fundamental Rights, lack of legislative competence and contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure. Mere disagreement with political policy is not by itself a ground.
accepted.tq: Exclude a political preference that is not a constitutional ground of review.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Supreme Court’s recognition of judicial review as part of the basic structure is associated particularly with
o: Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and L. Chandra Kumar, 1997
accepted.x: The basic-structure status of judicial review is associated with Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and was reaffirmed in the context of judicial review of tribunals in L. Chandra Kumar, 1997.
accepted.tq: Match the constitutional doctrine with its landmark cases and years.
accepted.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]
